A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DFR research by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison; rotated appendix tables were recovered and visually checked.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic linear and logistic experiments, interaction and cross-validation studies, and analyses of six real datasets in Sections 3–4 and Appendices D–E.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulation and real-data results in Sections 4–5 and Appendices D–E, including additional optimizer comparisons and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The two-stage screening algorithm, adaptive weights, objectives, and path initialization are retained. V2 corrects the documented aSGL KKT-violation condition from ≤ in v1 Equation 26 to > in v2 Equation 17, changing the stated condition for restoring discarded variables. The PDFs do not establish an underlying implementation change.

E1.justification: Both versions cover synthetic linear and logistic regression, even and uneven groups, second- and third-order interactions, and the same six real datasets. The BC-TGCA label in v1's appendix corresponds to brca1, not a removed dataset. Additional parameter and optimizer comparisons remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: Sparsegl and both GAP-safe variants remain evaluated, but their participation changes: GAP curves disappear from the dimensionality comparison (v1 Figure 1 versus v2 Figure 4) and appear in v2's alpha and signal-strength comparisons. V2 also adds the DFR-SGL BCD comparison variant in Figures 1–3 and Tables A5–A7.

E3.justification: V2 adds a BCD implementation of DFR as an optimizer control and new alpha/signal-strength comparisons using even groups of size 20. The earlier uneven-group sweeps remain separately reported. Path lengths, convergence tolerances, and 10-fold cross-validation are retained. Disclosure that GAP uses BCD does not establish a change to its earlier implementation.

E4.justification: V2 substantially extends investigation of the source of computational savings through the ATOS-versus-BCD control and component-level runtime breakdowns for synthetic data and scheetz (Tables A3–A4). Figure A4 also adds input-proportion sensitivity to adaptive-weight parameters. Conversely, pooling the appendix diagnostics removes much of the earlier sweep-specific detail.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 100 simulation repetitions, show 95% confidence intervals in simulation plots and standard errors in tables, and omit standard errors for whole-path real-data timings. No changed run count, seed policy, or uncertainty-estimation method is documented.

E6.justification: V2 adds BCD and runtime-breakdown results and replaces many separate simulation summaries with pooled results. Real-data measurements change substantially: DFR-aSGL's reported improvement factor changes from 23.19 to 685.08 on scheetz and from 900.39 to 81.48 on tumour (v1 Table A40; v2 Table A19). Active-set measurements also change without an explained cause, so these are revised results, not established same-setting performance gains. Interaction and cross-validation headline scores are retained.

T1.justification: V2 explicitly requires a differentiable, convex loss and revises sparsegl's Lipschitz derivation to operate on soft-thresholded gradients in Appendix C. It also corrects mathematical inequalities, including the aSGL violation test. Proposition 3.4 and Lemmas 3.5–3.6 largely formalize material already derived in v1 Appendix B.1; they are not new theoretical results.

C1.justification: V2 adds explicit priority claims that DFR supplies the first bi-level strong screening rules for SGL and the first screening rules for aSGL (Sections 1.2 and 6). The central claims of computational savings, two-stage screening, expanded tuning, and preserved solution optimality already appear in v1.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for optimizer robustness, the dimensionality-dependent screening pattern, and aSGL violations through adaptive-parameter dependence. Appendix D newly explains GAP's exclusion from uneven-group studies. The real-data interpretation shifts to convergence difficulties on scheetz and stronger penalization on adenoma, replacing v1's emphasis on trust-experts and celiac.

D1.justification: V2 newly identifies the dfr R package as available on CRAN, adds dataset download dates and the MSigDB access source, and distinguishes ATOS-specific settings from settings shared with BCD in Table A2. Most existing hyperparameters and data descriptions are retained; package availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for BCD, numerical-algorithm complexity, and the dfr package, while removing introductory OLS/ridge references. It sharpens DFR's novelty positioning through explicit first-method claims. The group-based SLOPE screening citation's transition from preprint to proceedings refers to the same work.

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and reorganized. V2 separates Preliminaries from Dual Feature Reduction, moves path-start material into the main text and pseudocode into the appendix, promotes existing adaptive-norm arguments into named results, and reorganizes the supplementary experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, reorganizes plot panels, adds screening-rule and runtime tables, and consolidates many appendix tables. Figure 10 combines the real-data path plots previously split between v1 Figure 5 and Figure A13. Real-data chart labeling is corrected, and several existing appendix displays move into the main text.

improvement.justification: The BCD control, measured screening overhead, and implementation access information strengthen evaluation and usability. V2 also repairs misleading real-data presentation: v1's claimed over-1000-fold gains on trust-experts and celiac conflict with Table A40, whereas v2's highlighted scheetz and adenoma gains agree with Table A19. These benefits are tempered by the loss of sweep-specific diagnostics and unexplained substantial replacements of real-data measurements.
